title: Peripatetic interpreters Alexander and Averroes; Pomponazzi; Galen vs Plato; Isidore of Pelusium
pass_a_gloss: Galen stood as indeed a most excellent man in philosophy and medicine, and an impious mocker belonging toward the doctrine belonging toward Moses, who even in On the Use belonging toward Parts book 10 dared to deny that God, if he wished, could make a horse or an ox from ashes — much more, as it seems, about to deny that the first man stood as produced from a clod belonging toward earth, or that the body belonging toward each man already reduced toward dust would stand as raised again the same in number. Oppose toward him what Isidore belonging toward Pelusium, the excellent disciple belonging toward the great Chrysostom, says against him in book 4, letter 125. Galen also either denied the immortality belonging toward the soul or called it into doubt. Both place outside man the agent intellect, which alone they admit to stand as immortal; toward which opinion belonging toward Averroes in the previous century Peter Pomponazzi alluded in disputing, and thereby provoked the censure belonging toward Pope Leo X in the Lateran Council, session 8. Next from the Peripatos there stand as two interpreters belonging toward Aristotle, one Greek — Alexander belonging toward Aphrodisias — the other Arab, namely Averroes.
pass_b_english: Next from the Peripatos there are two interpreters of Aristotle, one Greek — Alexander of Aphrodisias — the other Arab, namely Averroes: both place outside man the agent intellect, which alone they admit to be immortal; to which opinion of Averroes in the previous century Peter Pomponazzi alluded in disputing, and thereby provoked the censure of Pope Leo X in the Lateran Council, session 8. Galen also either denied the immortality of the soul or called it into doubt. For although somewhere he speaks so that he might seem less alien from admitting it, yet in the book That manners follow the temperament of the body he rebukes Plato for asserting the immortality of the mind.

Oppose to him what Isidore of Pelusium, the excellent disciple of the great Chrysostom, says against him in book 4, letter 125. Concerning the cure of bodies, he says, since that man is a most excellent craftsman in this art, let him speak by his own judgment: but concerning the soul let him not take up a contest with the wise nor descend into a struggle for which he is neither trained nor prepared. Galen was indeed a most excellent man in philosophy and medicine, and an impious mocker of the doctrine of Moses, who even in On the Use of Parts book 10 dared to deny that God, if he wished, could make a horse or an ox from ashes — much more, as it seems, about to deny that the first man was produced from a clod of earth, or that the body of each man already reduced to dust would be raised again the same in number.
source_text: Deinde ex Peripato duo sunt Aristotelis interpretes, unus Graecus Alexander Aphrodiseus, alter Arabs, nempe Averroes: uterque intellectum agentem, quem solum immortalem esse admittunt, extra hominem ponunt: ad quam opinionem Averrois superiore saeculo disputando allusit Petrus Pomponacius, quo censuram Leonis X. Pontificis in Concilio Lateranensi sess. 8. provocavit. Galenus quoque animae immortalitatem, vel negavit, vel in dubium vocavit. Nam etsi alicubi ita loquatur, ut ab ea admittenda minus alienus videri potuerit, tamen libro quod mores temperamentum corporis sequantur, Platonem ob assertam animi immortalitatem reprehendit. Cui oppone, quod Isidorus Pelusiotes, eximius magni Chrysostomi discipulus lib. 4. epist. 125. in eum dicit. De curatione corporum, inquiens, quoniam in hac arte excellens sum artifex vir ille, loquatur sane suo arbitratu: de anima vero certamen cum sapientibus ne suscipiat nec descendat in luctam, ad quam nec est exercitatus, nec praemeditatus. Galenus, vir quidem excellentissimus fuit in philosophia & Medicina, ac impius irrisor doctrinae Mosis, qui etiam lib. 10. de usu partium negare ausus fuit, Deum ex cineribus, si vellet, equum aut bovem facere posse, multo magis negaturus, ut videtur, hominem primum e gleba terrae fuisse productum, aut corpus hominis uniuscujusque in pulverem jam redactum idem numero resuscitandum iri.
